question: In a DNA molecule, which nitrogenous base always pairs with Adenine?
explanation: Think of Adenine and Thymine as best friends in the DNA structure—they always stick together! This pairing helps keep the DNA double helix nice and stable. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: What parts form the inner 'rungs' of the DNA ladder?
explanation: The outside of the DNA ladder is made of sugar and phosphate, but the steps you actually walk up on the inside are formed by pairs of nitrogenous bases. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: How many total chromosomes are in a normal human body (somatic) cell?
explanation: Normal human body cells have 46 chromosomes in total, neatly arranged in 23 pairs. You get 23 from mum and 23 from dad! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the main difference between an autosome and a sex chromosome in humans?

options.A: Autosomes exist as single strands rather than pairs
options.B: Autosomes do not determine biological sex like sex chromosomes do
options.C: Sex chromosomes carry no active protein-coding genes
options.D: Autosomes are only found in female cells

explanation: Out of your 23 pairs of chromosomes, 22 pairs are autosomes that handle your general body traits, while the last pair decides your biological sex. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h2)

question: What do we call a person who has two different alleles for a specific trait?
explanation: When the two gene copies are different (like one for brown eyes and one for blue), we call it heterozygous. 'Hetero' simply means different! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h3)

question: If a parent is a carrier for a dominant condition, what is the chance they will pass that gene to their child?
explanation: With dominant conditions, a parent with one affected gene has a fair 50-50 chance (one in two) of passing it on to their little one during fertilization. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h3)

question: Which inheritance pattern is shown by the AB human blood group?
explanation: Think of codominance like co-workers sharing the spotlight equally! In AB blood, both the A and B antigens show up proudly on the cell without hiding each other. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a feature of polygenic inheritance?

options.A: Controlled by a single gene pair
options.C: Applies to human traits like height
options.D: Produces a wide range of phenotypes

explanation: Poly- means many! Polygenic traits (like your height or skin color) are teamwork—controlled by many genes working together, not just a single pair. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h4)

question: What is it called when chromosomes fail to separate properly during cell division?
explanation: When chromosomes get stuck and refuse to separate ('non-disjunction'), cells end up with the wrong number of chromosomes, which can lead to conditions like Down syndrome. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h5)

question: What happens during a frameshift mutation in a gene sequence?

options.A: Doubling the total number of chromosomes in the nucleus
options.B: Shifting the nucleotide triplet reading frame during translation
options.C: Converting a DNA molecule directly into an RNA transcript
options.D: Stopping cellular division permanently at the G1 checkpoint

explanation: Imagine reading a three-letter sentence and accidentally deleting a letter—all the words after it shift and become gibberish! That's how a frameshift messes up protein building. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the genetic cause behind most cases of Down syndrome?
explanation: Trisomy 21 simply means there are three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the usual pair of two. You've got this! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why do males get X-linked recessive disorders like Hemophilia more often than females?

options.A: Maternal hormones protect female fetuses from inheriting defective alleles
options.B: The Y chromosome actively amplifies the expression of recessive mutations
options.C: Females lack the cellular machinery needed to transcribe X-linked genes
options.D: Males possess only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is fully expressed

explanation: Females have two X chromosomes, so a healthy backup X can often save the day. Males only have one X, so if there's a faulty gene there, they have no backup! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the main reason a nurse draws a genogram during a patient assessment?

options.A: To calculate exact medication dosages for genetic disorders
options.B: To measure the physical length of cellular chromosomes
options.C: To determine the precise blood pressure of family members
options.D: To map inherited health patterns across multiple generations

explanation: A genogram is like a detailed family tree that helps you spot health conditions running down through generations so you can care for your patient better. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h7)

question: When taking a family health history, what should a nurse look out for most?

options.C: Dietary preferences shared in the household

explanation: If a disease pops up unusually early in close family members (like heart trouble in someone very young), it's a big red flag for an inherited family risk. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h7)
